title: Death & the Brain / Paranormal Investigations
excerpt: Neurologist Dr. Tarvez Tucker discussed what medicine can observe at the edge of death. Followed by retired law enforcement investigator Larry Lawson, who shared how his police training has informed his approach to paranormal research.
content:
About the show

In the first half, neurologist Dr. Tarvez Tucker discussed what medicine can observe at the edge of death, drawing from 15 years treating patients with severe brain injuries. She explained that new EEG technology has captured brain activity after cardiac and cerebral arrest. "We actually see some fast gamma activity, which can be associated with perception after death occurs," she revealed. She distinguished these experiences from ordinary dreams, observing that "the lucid memories that people have after or during near-death experiences are very clear. They're very detailed. They're precise."

Across cultures, she noted, near-death survivors report four consistent elements: a bright light, an out-of-body sensation, a life review, and a feeling of peace while reuniting with deceased loved ones. "No matter where you live, what culture you're from, what religion you are... these [are] universal experiences after death," Tucker remarked. She also addressed the eerie "Lazarus sign," in which bodies already declared brain dead suddenly sit up. "It happens in people with absolutely no brain activity whatsoever," she explained, describing it as a spinal reflex rather than a sign of life.

Tucker warned that apparent death can sometimes be reversible. She called opioid overdoses and hypothermia "death chameleons," conditions in which a person may appear lifeless but can recover with treatment. She also described terminal lucidity, when a person with advanced dementia briefly regains recognition and clarity. According to Tucker, this phenomenon is emotionally powerful but often signals that death is near. When asked whether she believed in an afterlife, she expressed uncertainty. "I don't think anyone can know that yet," she reflected, "but I think this gives us a window into promising research for the future."

-------------------

In the second half, retired law enforcement investigator Larry Lawson shared how his police training has informed his approach to paranormal research. "To be a good investigator, you have to have an open mind," Lawson explained. "You've got to... look at the evidence, and make a decision based upon the evidence. Well, the paranormal is no different." He traced his interest in the supernatural to an early experience as a 20-year-old officer at the Dade County Jail in Miami. While working in a control booth, he recalled seeing a tall, unknown uniformed figure walking along a secured catwalk. Other officers reportedly searched the area and found no one. "I know what I saw," Lawson asserted.

A second encounter at the St. Augustine Lighthouse in 2010 prompted him to investigate the subject more seriously. During a nighttime tour with his son, Lawson recounted that they heard children laughing on the lighthouse's fourth floor, despite finding no speakers or other apparent source. "There was nothing that could have replicated what we heard," he added. He eventually founded the Florida Bureau of Paranormal Investigation and later created Indian River Haunting, a guided tour that combines local history, legends, and cases examined by his team.

He described one case in Sebastian, Florida, involving alleged communication with a 5-year-old girl named Belinda. A medium reportedly identified the child's name and age during an investigation, and Lawson later located a nearby grave for a 5-year-old Belinda who died in 1939. He said the case raised suspicions of foul play but remained unresolved. "That's the type of case... that keeps me going," Lawson said.

News segment guests: Lauren Weinstein, Robert Zimmerman
